explanations.answer: Agree with each other in the Lord
explanations.explanation: That's it, baker. Paul writes, "I urge Euodia and Syntyche to agree with each other in the Lord." (Philippians 4:2) Euodia and Syntyche were two women in the church at Philippi. Notice he says "in the Lord," so the agreeing happens with Him in the middle. I think that's a good recipe for any disagreement.

explanations.answer: Come and visit him right away
explanations.explanation: Nice try, friend, but there's no visit in this verse. Paul urges Euodia and Syntyche "to agree with each other in the Lord." (Philippians 4:2) The request is about how they get along, not where they travel. I'd have loved a surprise visit myself back in that drawer, but nobody ever came by except for scissors.

explanations.answer: Choose new leaders for the church
explanations.explanation: Not this one, baker. Paul never mentions picking leaders here. He says, "I urge Euodia and Syntyche to agree with each other in the Lord." (Philippians 4:2) The whole ask is about the two of them agreeing, nothing about a vote or a new lineup.

True, baker! Paul says, "I ask you, my true yokefellow, to help these women who have contended at my side for the gospel." (Philippians 4:3) The writer doesn't name this yokefellow, so we leave the name blank too. A yokefellow is someone yoked alongside you, pulling the same load. Euodia and Syntyche get named, and this helper gets the job.

Not quite, friend. The text says, "I ask you, my true yokefellow, to help these women who have contended at my side for the gospel." (Philippians 4:3) So Paul does ask for help, and the women he means are Euodia and Syntyche from the verse before. Easy one to second-guess when the yokefellow has no name attached.

explanations.answer: Worked at his side to spread the gospel
explanations.explanation: Right on, baker. Paul calls them women "who have contended at my side for the gospel." (Philippians 4:3) They didn't watch from the sidelines. They were in it right next to Paul. That's a compliment worth framing, and I'd frame it next to my best batch.

explanations.answer: Carried his letters to the other churches
explanations.explanation: Good guess, but the text doesn't say that about these two. Paul says they "have contended at my side for the gospel." (Philippians 4:3) Nothing about delivering letters. I'd leave the mail route out of it, since the verse only says they stood with him for the gospel.

explanations.answer: Taught the new believers in their homes
explanations.explanation: Close to something that sounds right, friend, but this verse doesn't say it. Paul says these women "have contended at my side for the gospel." (Philippians 4:3) That's all the text gives us about their work. I won't guess at more than Paul wrote.

Ooh, not this time, baker. Paul says, "Rejoice in the Lord always. I will say it again: Rejoice!" (Philippians 4:4) The word is "always," and there's no "only when things go well" tucked in there. He says it twice, so he means it.
False is right, baker! Paul writes, "Rejoice in the Lord always." (Philippians 4:4) He doesn't add any conditions, and he says it twice. Always means always, even on a burnt-batch kind of day.

Yes, baker! Paul writes, "Let your gentleness be apparent to all." (Philippians 4:5) Apparent means other people can see it. Gentleness isn't something to stash in the back of the pantry. Put it out front where everyone can see it.

Wisdom is a great thing, friend, but it's not the word here. Paul says, "Let your gentleness be apparent to all." (Philippians 4:5) The word is gentleness. Wisdom shows up in plenty of other places, just not in this verse.

Strength sounds like a fine answer, baker, but Paul picked a different word. He says, "Let your gentleness be apparent to all." (Philippians 4:5) Gentleness is the one he wants everybody to see. I'll admit it surprised me too.

Not this time, baker. Paul says, "Be anxious for nothing." (Philippians 4:6) Nothing means nothing, so he doesn't leave a short list of approved worries. Instead he points to prayer, which is what the rest of the verse is about.

False is right, friend. Paul says, "Be anxious for nothing, but in everything, by prayer and petition, with thanksgiving, present your requests to God." (Philippians 4:6) No exceptions made for the big stuff or the small stuff. Everything goes to God in prayer.

explanations.answer: Present them to God with thanksgiving
explanations.explanation: That's the one, baker. Paul says, "in everything, by prayer and petition, with thanksgiving, present your requests to God." (Philippians 4:6) Notice the thanksgiving rides along with the asking. Every request goes straight to God Himself.

explanations.answer: Leave them unspoken and trust God
explanations.explanation: Close, but not what Paul says, friend. He tells them, "by prayer and petition, with thanksgiving, present your requests to God." (Philippians 4:6) The requests get spoken, not left unsaid. He tells them to bring the requests right to God.

explanations.answer: Present them to the elders with fasting
explanations.explanation: Good try, baker, but that's not in this verse. Paul says, "present your requests to God," and he adds "by prayer and petition, with thanksgiving." (Philippians 4:6) The requests go to God, and thanksgiving is the companion, not fasting.

True, baker! Paul says, "the peace of God, which surpasses all understanding, will guard your hearts and your minds in Christ Jesus." (Philippians 4:7) Guard is a strong word. I think of a doorkeeper standing watch over the whole place, and it all happens in Christ Jesus.

Not quite, friend. Paul really does say it: "the peace of God, which surpasses all understanding, will guard your hearts and your minds in Christ Jesus." (Philippians 4:7) Both hearts and minds get guarded. It's a promise, not a maybe.

You got it, baker! Paul says, "think on these things." (Philippians 4:8) After the whole list of true, honorable, right, pure, lovely and admirable, the instruction is to think. Fill the mind with the good stuff, like filling a cookie box with the good batch.

Good guess, friend, since waiting shows up in the Bible a lot. But here Paul says, "think on these things." (Philippians 4:8) He wants the believers to put their minds on that list of good things. No waiting required.

Counting is a fine hobby, baker. I've counted plenty of dust specks myself. But Paul's word here is "think." He says, "think on these things." (Philippians 4:8) The list is meant for the mind to dwell on, not to tally.

Yes, baker! Paul says, "Whatever you have learned or received or heard from me, or seen in me, put it into practice." (Philippians 4:9) Learning is only half the batch. The other half is doing it. Then comes the promise: "the God of peace will be with you."

Good thought, but Paul asks for more than remembering, friend. He says, "Whatever you have learned or received or heard from me, or seen in me, put it into practice." (Philippians 4:9) Knowing a recipe doesn't fill the box. You have to bake it.

Nice idea, baker, but that's not what this verse says. Paul says, "put it into practice." (Philippians 4:9) The action is for the believers themselves to live it out. Passing it along isn't in the text here.
